articles.title: One vote, 450 Years: Africa rewrites the world map
articles.author: Ruth Wacuka
articles.authorBio: Ruth Wacuka writes for The Nile Explorer.

image.alt: A full United Nations General Assembly hall, the speaker at the podium also shown on two large screens flanking the UN emblem.
image.caption: Robert Dussey, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Togo, at the podium and on the screens, introduces the “Correct the map” draft resolution.

blocks.text: A wall map has hung in classrooms across this continent for decades, in Lagos, in Lusaka, in Nairobi, in a thousand rooms nobody bothered to name. Laminated, curling at the edges, it shows Africa squeezed into a shape barely larger than Greenland, which floats above it near the Arctic Circle. No child is ever told to question it. A map is not handed to a child as an argument to be tested; it is handed over as a fact, in the same register as the multiplication table. Generations grew up carrying that shape of the world inside them. The shape they carried was false.

For four hundred and fifty years, the world’s default picture of itself rendered Africa, a continent large enough to hold the United States, China, India, Japan and most of Europe, with room left over, as smaller than Greenland, a slab of Arctic ice with a population you could fit inside a single African city. Nobody sat down in 1569 and voted to shrink a continent out of malice. Gerardus Mercator was solving a sailor’s problem, not writing a doctrine. But doctrines do not always announce themselves. Sometimes they are simply inherited, generation after generation, until a lie grows old enough to wear the clothes of fact.
On 4 September 2026, at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, 164 countries said otherwise. Out loud. On the record.

The resolution is called “Correct the Map.” It is an African-led campaign, run by African civil society, adopted by the African Union, and carried to the floor by an African state, and it won a vote at the highest table in global governance. Togo brought the resolution on behalf of the African Group, all fifty-four member states, with the AU’s backing behind it. It passed 164 to 1. The United States cast the lone vote against, calling the resolution an “ideological agenda” and a distraction from “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations.” Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine abstained. Everyone else put a hand up and confessed that the map was never true, and that the world had long known it.
A map that did not matter would not be worth a formal no on the world stage. The objection was itself a confession.

This is the era Africa is currently living through. For six decades, the continent won its flags, its anthems, its seats at the table. What it is winning now is something harder to hand over in a ceremony, which is the right to describe itself. A new generation of Pan-Africanists is doing what Nkrumah and Lumumba were doing before anyone thought to call it a movement, turning back to the archive, the textbook, the atlas and the museum shelf, and asking the same blunt question of each one: who wrote this, and on whose authority? Africa is not simply demanding a bigger seat in rooms built by other people. It is asking who drew the room, who decided its dimensions, and why nobody thought to check.

The conversation did not start at the UN. It started with a map on a wall, and with two African advocacy organisations, Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa, who launched what they first called the “Change the Map” campaign, later rebranded “Correct the Map.” Their argument had been made for years by geographers and educators, but rarely with this much organising behind it. The Mercator projection, designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European sailors hold a straight compass bearing at sea, was never built to teach a child what the world looks like. It became the default map anyway, in classrooms, atlases and newsrooms, and it shrinks Africa dramatically while inflating Europe and North America.

The distortion is not so much a flaw as a trade-off that nobody outside cartography ever gets told about. Any flat map of a round planet has to sacrifice something, because you cannot preserve shape, area and direction all at once, so every projection is really a choice about which lie to tell. Mercator chose to preserve angles and shape, because a sailor needs a straight line on paper to hold a straight compass bearing at sea. The cost of that choice is area, and the cost grows the further you travel from the equator. Landmasses near the poles balloon far beyond their true size, while landmasses near the equator, where most of Africa sits, are rendered smaller than they are. This is why Canada, Russia and Greenland dominate a Mercator map out of all proportion to their populations or land area, and why Africa, India and Indonesia consistently read as smaller than the reality. On a Mercator map, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers roughly 30.3 million square kilometres against Greenland’s 2.2 million, which makes Africa about fourteen times larger.

Fara Ndiaye, co-founder of Speak Up Africa, put the stakes plainly. A generation raised on a distorted map absorbs a distorted sense of Africa’s economic, demographic and strategic weight. Moky Makura of Africa No Filter called it what it is, not a cartographic error but a narrative one. The campaign’s ask was institutional, that schools, media houses, the UN, the World Bank and the BBC adopt the Equal Earth projection instead, a map developed by geographers in 2018 that makes the opposite trade-off to Mercator’s. It preserves each landmass’s true relative size at the cost of slightly bending shape and angle, which is a fair exchange for a wall map or a classroom atlas that will never need to plot a ship’s course. Selma Malika Haddadi, speaking for the AU, made the point that has anchored the campaign since. Africa is the world’s second largest continent, and a map that visually erases that fact shapes how the world negotiates with it, invests in it and thinks about it.

Togo’s Foreign Minister, Robert Dussey, framed it on the floor of the General Assembly in a single line worth remembering. “A fair world begins with a fair map.” He was direct about where the responsibility sat. “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.” France announced on the spot that it would retire Mercator for Equal Earth. Togo says it will update its own school geography materials before the year is out. None of this is binding. No country is required to burn an old atlas, and Mercator still does, competently, the one job it was built for, which is helping a ship hold a straight line at sea. What the vote does is put the UN’s institutional weight behind a truer default, and dare the world’s cartographers, publishers and ministries of education to follow.

Here is the uncomfortable part of the story. No single figure sat down in 1569 and voted to shrink a continent, and that is precisely what makes this kind of distortion so difficult to undo. Mercator was solving a narrow, genuine problem, not writing a doctrine. A single villain can be named, tried and removed. A structure that reproduces the same convenient lie for centuries, with the benefit spread just widely enough that no one institution ever has to answer for the whole of it, is far harder to dislodge. Colonial administrations adopted his projection and exported it to the territories they governed, not by accident but because a continent that looked smaller was easier to carve up, easier to govern from a distance and easier to justify governing at all. A tool built for European sailors became the map European schools taught, which became the map colonial administrations exported, which became the default that humanity inherited. Nobody re-litigated the choice for four hundred and fifty years or more. It calcified into how the world looks, which is precisely how the most durable distortions survive, through nobody ever being handed a reason to ask why it was drawn that way.

The map was never an isolated invention. It arrived as part of a much larger apparatus, one that needed Africa to appear smaller, emptier and less consequential than it was, because a diminished continent was easier to carve up, easier to govern from a distance and easier to justify governing at all. Colonialism did not simply draw borders through African communities with a ruler and a pen. It authored an entire vocabulary for how the continent would be seen, measured and spoken about, as a landmass to be extracted from rather than a civilisation to be reckoned with, as a set of tribes rather than nations, as a blank space waiting to be filled in by someone else’s history. The map was simply the most literal expression of a habit that ran through everything, which was to shrink the subject and make the taking easier to live with.

That is the deeper question this vote forces into the open. If something as measurable, as checkable, as a continent’s actual surface area could go uncorrected for four and a half centuries, accepted without challenge by geographers, publishers, ministries of education and the UN itself, what else has the world simply decided not to verify? What else has this continent inherited without ever demanding the receipts? Makura asked almost exactly that once the vote had passed. If the world got something this basic wrong for this long, what else about Africa has it accepted without question? She was precise about one thing, and the precision matters. This was never a campaign to inflate Africa. “Africa doesn’t need to be made bigger. It needs to be seen accurately.”The distinction is the whole argument. The campaign was never asking the world to exaggerate a continent’s importance, only to stop deflating it by default.

A map is never neutral. Dussey said as much on the floor of the Assembly, that it shapes perception before anyone is old enough to argue with it, and that it teaches how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood. Size, on a map, reads as a proxy for significance. A continent drawn smaller than it is gets treated as smaller than it is, in classrooms, in newsroom decisions about what counts as global news, in the boardroom logic that still underprices African markets relative to their scale. The distortion was cartographic. The consequences were economic, political and psychological. This vote is one thread in a larger reckoning the continent is currently having with itself. The African Union named 2025 its Theme of the Year, Justice for Africans and People of African Descent through Reparations, and folded Correct the Map into that agenda as a flagship outcome. Reparations, read this way, is not only about ledgers and compensation. It is about correcting the record everywhere the record was falsified, including the one that hung on a classroom wall.

The clearest articulation of the stakes came months before the UN vote, at the 9th Pan-African Congress in Lomé, held under the theme Renewal of Pan-Africanism and Africa’s Role in the Reform of Multilateral Institutions. It reframes the whole campaign away from convincing the world and toward something more internal, which is generations of Africans, educated on the same distorted map as everyone else, absorbing a diminished sense of their own continent’s scale and weight. Pan-Africanism has always argued that liberation has to happen in the mind before it can happen anywhere else. This is that argument applied to something as unglamorous as a wall chart. The Congress closed with three concrete tasks. Sign the petition, audit the maps in your own schools and offices and demand correction where they are wrong. Mobilise your networks, because, as the closing line put it, change starts with us. That is the same posture Dussey carried to the UN floor months later, a statement of intent that Africa would fix what it could fix itself, and invite the rest of the world to follow if it chose to.

It would be easy to file this under symbolism and move on. That would be a mistake. Power is not only held in treaties, currencies and militaries. It is held in the frames through which the world is taught to see itself. A map is a frame. For half a millennium, that frame told every schoolchild on earth, African and non-African alike, that Africa was smaller and therefore lesser. It told policymakers the same thing before they ever opened a trade brief.

What makes this moment worth marking is not the map itself. It is the sequence. This was not a resolution handed down from above and accepted quietly. It is the spirit of Pan-Africanism this vote actually embodies, not a grievance lodged with the world but Africans setting the terms of their own representation and building the coalition to make it hold. The resolution in New York does not undo four hundred and fifty years of inheritance but it does something a resolution rarely manages. It hands every teacher, every publisher and every parent standing in front of a child and a wall map a reason, finally and officially, to ask why it was ever drawn that way, and to put something truer up in its place.

None of this is new territory for the continent’s own thinkers. Sons of the continent, figures like PLO Lumumba, were already asking, in lecture halls and on public platforms across Africa, why the continent keeps inheriting other people’s descriptions of itself without ever being asked to check them, its history, its economics, its very geography, handed down as settled fact rather than something to interrogate. Kwame Nkrumah said it plainer still, decades before any of this had a hashtag, that Africa’s independence would mean nothing if it left the continent’s mind still colonised. The map is simply the version of that argument you can hold up and measure with a ruler. Most of the others are not so easily proven, which may be exactly why they have lasted longer.

The real work now sits in the classroom wall, the textbook printer and the newsroom map graphic. Whether ministries of education from Nairobi to Kigali to Juba actually replace those maps is the next test.

But the map was the easy one, a single, checkable fact, wrong for 450 years and finally corrected by a vote. What other stories, statistics and assumptions about this continent has the world simply accepted without challenging, and how many of them has Africa accepted about itself? Every generation gets one chance to stop inheriting the answers it was never allowed to question. This is Africa’s.

articles.summary: A wall map has hung in classrooms across this continent for decades, in Lagos, in Lusaka, in Nairobi, in a thousand rooms nobody bothered to name.

articles.title: Kenya’s Expulsion of Small Traders Exposes Africa’s Unpreparedness for Visa-Free Borders
articles.author: Kirangacha Mwaniki
articles.authorBio: Kirangacha Mwaniki is CEO of Virtue Book Publishers and Executive Director of Virtue Literacy Africa. He writes on publishing, literacy, and African governance.

image.alt: A busy Nairobi street lined with small shops and market stalls, a motorcycle taxi riding towards the camera.
image.caption: Jamhuri Estate — a bustling street that is home to a large community of Ethiopian, Eritrean and South Sudanese immigrants, September 2026

blocks.text: Kenya’s President William Ruto has stirred considerable controversy across the region with an unprecedented directive targeting small-scale foreign traders accused of occupying business niches long considered the preserve of ordinary Kenyans. On September 2, 2026, addressing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise traders at State House, Ruto ordered foreign nationals operating hawking businesses and small retail shops to close down, insisting that Kenya’s visa-free entry and investment climate were built for investors to come to Kenya, not hawkers and traders. Enforcement began on September 7, though the government later softened the blanket closure into a 90-day window for affected foreigners to regularise their immigration, work permit, and business registration status.

The directive sent shockwaves across estates and business districts where foreign nationals have long run modest enterprises, with many opting to shutter their shops and stay behind closed doors rather than risk confrontation with enforcement officers. Jamhuri Estate, a middle-income neighbourhood on Nairobi’s western side long associated with a sizeable Ethiopian and Eritrean community, saw many residents retreat indoors for fear of arrest and harassment by opportunistic law enforcement. The anxiety was not confined to Nairobi’s estates alone. Burundian nationals gathered in numbers at their embassy seeking travel documents, prompting Kenya’s own Foreign Affairs establishment to issue a formal apology to the Burundian community for the harassment experienced amid the confusion, while Kenya’s ambassador to Burundi moved to reassure Kenyans living there of their own safety in turn.

Yet even as the directive was widely misunderstood and, in places, misapplied, the underlying rationale offered by a president who has otherwise been among the continent’s most vocal champions of a borderless Africa deserves closer scrutiny than it has so far received.
A Structural Gap

The clearest lesson to emerge from this episode is that African governments have moved faster in their political enthusiasm for visa-free movement than in building the administrative machinery required to manage it. Many have competed, sometimes emotionally, to open their borders to fellow Africans as a symbol of continental solidarity and economic integration. Far fewer have built the immigration infrastructure needed to distinguish, at entry, between a tourist, an investor, and an informal trader intending to set up shop without registration, tax compliance, or adherence to basic health and safety standards.

blocks.alt: Two people bent over a cart of folded clothes on a residential street, a third walking away in the background.
blocks.caption: A Burundian hawker plies his trade on Nairobi streets

blocks.text: Kenya’s own immigration points appear to lack a clear system for ascertaining the specific purpose of travel and, where business is declared as that purpose, for channelling arrivals into a defined registration process with clear requirements around tax compliance, licensing, and safety standards. On this front, Ruto appears to have been caught flat-footed by a consequence of policy his own government helped create. Having championed visa-free entry as a marker of Pan-African progress, the administration seems to have moved ahead of the regulatory scaffolding needed to manage its effects, only to respond after the fact with a blunt administrative directive rather than the structural fix the situation actually calls for.
Tax, Employment, and Capital Flight

Economists who have weighed in on the matter point to a second, more material concern. Visa-free entry, absent proper oversight, carries real risk of capital drain. Many small-scale foreign traders operating informally in Kenya have not been paying taxes, nor are they generating meaningful local employment. Proceeds from the sale of imported merchandise are frequently wired directly back to support families in traders’ home countries rather than being reinvested locally. In some cases, the goods themselves, peanuts, cassava, and other agricultural produce among them, are imported from traders’ countries of origin, meaning the economic activity strengthens farming and production economies elsewhere on the continent rather than in Kenya. The net effect, critics argue, is a pattern of extraction rather than exchange: informal cross-border trade that benefits the trader’s home economy while contributing little in tax revenue, job creation, or reinvestment to the host country.
Reciprocity and the Currency Question

A third concern, raised by many ordinary Kenyans watching the debate unfold, centres on reciprocity and currency flow. While the spirit of a borderless Africa rightly holds that Africans should be free to live, work, and trade across the continent, the absence of preparedness measures means that countries with comparatively stronger currencies risk disproportionate cash outflows when informal traders use locally earned income to sustain households and economies back home rather than circulating that income within the host economy. Free movement without coordinated fiscal and monetary safeguards can, in effect, become a one-directional transfer of value rather than the mutual economic integration the African Union’s free movement protocols were designed to achieve.

blocks.alt: A row of small shopfronts with signs in Amharic script, motorcycle taxis parked outside and a food stall under a yellow umbrella.
blocks.caption: Jamhuri Estate — an Ethiopian business strip in the heart of Nairobi

blocks.text: Whatever the merits or excesses of Ruto’s specific directive, and there have clearly been real harms in its implementation, from harassment of documented foreign nationals to diplomatic strain with neighbouring states, the episode has surfaced a truth that African governments can no longer avoid. The political will for a borderless Africa has consistently outpaced the administrative readiness to manage what open borders actually require: functioning immigration data systems, clear business registration pathways for foreign entrepreneurs, coordinated tax and labour policy, and regional agreements on capital flow and reciprocity. Kenya’s own government has since walked back the harsher edges of the directive, extending a 90-day regularisation window and instructing security agencies to protect documented foreign nationals from arbitrary mistreatment. But the underlying gap the episode exposed will not close on its own.

If the African Union’s vision of free movement is to mean more than the removal of visa stickers at the border, it must be matched by the unglamorous work of building the systems, immigration, taxation, business licensing, and monetary coordination, that make free movement sustainable rather than combustible. Kenya’s experience this September should serve as a warning to every government on the continent still celebrating visa-free entry as an end in itself rather than the beginning of a much harder institutional task.

articles.title: Beyond Majority Rule: The Case for Pan-African Democracy
articles.author: Kirangacha Mwaniki
articles.authorBio: Kirangacha Mwaniki is CEO of Virtue Book Publishers and Executive Director of Virtue Literacy Africa. He writes on publishing, literacy, and African governance.

image.alt: A near-empty House of Commons chamber, one member speaking at the despatch box with others spaced along the green benches.
image.caption: The House of Commons in session

blocks.text: Liberal democracy as a system of governance has long been championed by Western powers and their allies, and in many cases strongly imposed on African countries during and after the colonial period, a push that frequently put newly independent administrations at odds with the very populations they governed. This external pressure contributed, in numerous instances, to the birth of new constitutions that shifted greater power to citizens by enshrining individual rights and freedoms. On paper, liberal democracy is a compelling framework. It combines majority rule with protections for minority rights and individual freedoms, resting on a set of core values: majority rule, where citizens vote to choose leaders and the side with the most votes wins; minority rights, where laws protect those who do not belong to the winning group; rule of law, where government and citizen alike are bound by the same legal standards; free and fair elections, allowing leaders to be changed peacefully through regular, open contests; and individual freedoms, including speech, press, and religion.
The difficulty is not with these principles in the abstract. The difficulty is with how they arrived in Africa, and with what was left out along the way.
A System Imposed

Much of liberal democracy’s implementation across African regimes came bundled with intimidation, coercion, and considerable imbalance, as departing colonial administrations and their successors worked to ensure that their preferred governance model took root, regardless of whether the societies inheriting it had been given the space to adapt it to their own political realities. Among the five pillars listed above, majority rule took centre stage in this push. Western governments and international institutions have consistently emphasised free and fair elections as the measure of democratic legitimacy, while paying comparatively little attention to the social and political conditions that determine what happens once the votes are counted.

This is where the liberal democratic model, transplanted wholesale onto the African continent, begins to strain. It is widely observed that many African nations remain deeply structured around ethnic identity and communal belonging, and that this reality shapes how people organise themselves politically far more than ideology or policy platforms do. Political parties across much of the continent are frequently built around ethnic or regional coalitions rather than around a coherent, rational, issue-based vision for governance. It is not uncommon to see political leaders mobilise the public along ethnic lines, absent any clear articulation of leadership vision or policy direction, and then present that ethnic coalition at the ballot box as a legitimate majority, entitled to invoke the language of free and fair elections to claim power.

This is the gap that liberal democracy, as exported to Africa, has consistently failed to close. A system built on the premise that the majority’s will should govern says very little about how that majority is formed, or whether its formation serves the collective interest of the nation or merely the sectional interest of whichever ethnic bloc manages to out-organise its rivals. African democracies, in many cases, have ended up crowded with corruption, brutality, and intimidation by ruling elites who understood early that liberal democracy’s procedural safeguards could be satisfied on paper while its deeper spirit, government by and for the whole people, was hollowed out in practice.
What Majority Rule Was Never Meant to Be

Majority rule must never be reduced to a mechanism by which sectional or even hostile groupings assemble sufficient numbers to seize leadership in pursuit of narrow, individual, or ethnic interest. Democracy, properly understood, must be anchored in ideologies and platforms that advance the interests of an entire nation, not merely the interests of whichever coalition happens to command a plurality on election day. Liberal democracy scores well on several fronts, protection of individual liberties, the rule of law, freedom of expression, but it falls flat precisely where Africa needs it most: in ensuring that the process by which a majority is formed reflects genuine national deliberation rather than ethnic arithmetic.
This is precisely the space Pan-African democracy is positioned to fill.

Pan-African democracy does not reject the values liberal democracy claims to uphold, rule of law, protection of rights, peaceful transfer of power. What it rejects is the assumption that the ballot box, on its own, is a sufficient mechanism for translating those values into legitimate governance in societies still organised significantly along ethnic and communal lines. Long before the colonial encounter, African societies across the continent had developed their own sophisticated systems of collective governance: councils of elders who deliberated until consensus was reached rather than simply tallying votes, communal assemblies where every lineage or clan had a voice in decisions affecting the whole, and mechanisms of accountability rooted in kinship, custom, and communal legitimacy rather than in periodic elections alone. These systems were not perfect, and no serious case for Pan-African democracy should romanticise them uncritically. But they shared a common insight that liberal democracy’s majoritarian model too often ignores: that legitimate governance requires the active inclusion and buy-in of all significant constituent groups, not merely the temporary alliance of whichever coalition can muster fifty percent plus one.

A Pan-African democratic model, then, would draw on this indigenous inheritance while retaining what liberal democracy genuinely gets right. It would combine free and fair elections with deliberate, constitutionally embedded mechanisms for power-sharing and consensus-building across ethnic and regional lines, ensuring that no single group can capture the state entirely on the strength of numbers alone. It would insist that political parties organise around ideology and policy platforms rather than ethnic mobilisation, using legal and institutional levers, campaign finance rules, party registration requirements, civic education, to actively discourage the ethnic coalition-building that has hollowed out liberal democracy’s promise across the continent. And it would treat minority protection not merely as a constitutional afterthought bolted onto a majoritarian system, but as a structural feature of how power itself is organised and exercised.

blocks.alt: A man in a dark suit speaking from a lectern bearing the European Parliament emblem, the EU flag behind him.
blocks.caption: President William Ruto addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg

blocks.text: It is worth acknowledging, honestly, that consensus and power-sharing models have not always delivered on their promise elsewhere on the continent. Critics point to Uganda’s Movement System of the 1980s and 1990s, which was framed as a homegrown alternative to divisive multi-party competition but was widely seen, over time, to have entrenched a single leadership well beyond what genuine consensus-building would justify. Rwanda’s post-1994 governance arrangements are cited in similarly divided terms, credited by some for rebuilding national unity after genocide through deliberate power-sharing and reconciliation structures, while criticised by others as a framework that has, in practice, narrowed political space and shielded incumbency from serious challenge. These examples are a legitimate caution, not a rebuttal. They demonstrate that any model built around consensus and inclusion, Pan-African or otherwise, can be captured by the same elites it was designed to restrain, if it is not paired with genuine institutional accountability, term limits, and independent oversight. The answer is not to abandon the search for a governance model suited to Africa’s social realities, but to build one with these historical cautionary tales in view, rather than repeating them.
Which Way Africa Chooses

None of this amounts to a rejection of democracy itself, nor a case for authoritarianism dressed in African garb, a trap some regimes have historically used to justify entrenchment and abuse. It is, instead, a case for democratic maturity: a recognition that the specific procedural form liberal democracy took in the West, one shaped by centuries of its own political development, including the gradual, often painful management of its internal divisions, cannot simply be transplanted onto societies with a fundamentally different social architecture and be expected to function identically. Africa does not need to import a finished product. It needs the space and the confidence to build governance systems that take seriously both the values liberal democracy espouses and the social realities liberal democracy, as practised on the continent, has too often failed to reckon with.

The case for Pan-African democracy, then, is not a case against the ballot box. It is a case for what must surround the ballot box if it is to produce governments that serve the whole nation rather than merely the winning coalition. That is the unfinished work liberal democracy left behind in Africa, and it is the work Pan-African democracy must now take up.
